title: How Elevators Know Which Floor to Stop At
excerpt: An elevator never sees a floor. It compares measured position data with your request and slows down before it arrives.
imageAlt: Illustration for How Elevators Know Which Floor to Stop At
content:
When you enter an elevator and press a floor button, the lift seems to understand your request immediately. It closes its doors, starts moving, slows down at the right moment, and stops exactly where you selected. But how does it know which floor to reach, and how does it avoid stopping at every floor along the way?

Modern elevators use a combination of sensors, control systems, position detectors, and motor technology to manage every movement. The process is much more organized than simply following button presses.

The Elevator Records Your Floor Selection

Every time someone presses a floor button, the request is sent to the elevator's control system. This system acts like the elevator's decision-making center.

It records the selected floor and keeps track of other requests made by passengers. For example, if someone on the second floor selects the seventh floor while another passenger on the fifth floor selects the ninth, the system considers both requests when deciding how to operate.

In buildings with several elevators, a central controller may also decide which lift should respond to a passenger's call. This helps reduce unnecessary travel and waiting time.

Sensors Tell the Elevator Where It Is

An elevator cannot rely on guesswork to determine its position. It uses position sensors and other monitoring devices to track its location inside the elevator shaft.

Depending on the elevator design, these systems may use magnetic sensors, optical devices, encoders, or other position-detection technology. They identify the elevator's position and help the controller measure how far it has travelled.

The control system also monitors movement speed and direction. This information allows it to calculate when the elevator needs to slow down before reaching the selected floor.

The Control System Decides When to Stop

The elevator's controller continuously compares its current position with the requested destination.

Suppose you select the eighth floor while standing on the ground floor. The controller knows the destination, monitors the lift's movement, and adjusts its operation as it approaches the target.

It does not simply wait until the elevator reaches the eighth floor before stopping the motor. Instead, it begins reducing speed in advance so the lift can reach the correct level smoothly.

This controlled slowdown is important because an elevator needs to align its floor with the building's landing. Even a small difference in height can make entering or leaving the lift uncomfortable or unsafe.

Why Elevators Sometimes Stop at Other Floors

You may have noticed an elevator stopping at a floor even though you did not press its button. This usually happens because another passenger has requested that floor.

Many elevators follow a direction-based scheduling system. When travelling upward, the controller may serve passengers who have requested higher floors before reversing direction to handle downward requests.

This approach reduces unnecessary changes in direction and makes the journey more efficient.

More advanced elevator systems can group passengers according to their destinations. In busy buildings, destination-control systems may ask passengers to select their floor before entering the elevator and then assign them to a particular lift.

Safety Systems Check Every Movement

Stopping at the correct floor is only one part of elevator operation. The control system also monitors door positions, speed, motor performance, and other safety conditions.

For example, door sensors can detect an obstruction and prevent the doors from closing normally. Overspeed protection systems can respond if the elevator moves faster than its permitted limit. Other safety mechanisms help prevent the lift from travelling beyond its intended operating range.

These systems work together so that the elevator does not depend on a single sensor or instruction.

A Small Computer Coordinates the Entire Journey

An elevator may look like a simple box moving between floors, but its operation involves several systems communicating continuously.

The buttons record passenger requests, sensors track the elevator's position, the controller manages speed and direction, and safety devices monitor whether movement can continue.

That is how an elevator knows when to stop. It is not recognizing floors by sight. It is following carefully measured position data and instructions from its control system, allowing it to reach the correct floor smoothly and safely.

faq.q: How does an elevator know where it is in the shaft?
faq.a: Position sensors such as magnetic, optical or encoder-based devices track its location and how far it has travelled.

faq.q: Why does an elevator stop at floors I did not press?
faq.a: Another passenger has requested that floor. Many elevators serve requests in the direction they are already travelling.

faq.q: Does an elevator brake only when it reaches the floor?
faq.a: No. The controller begins reducing speed ahead of time so the car can level smoothly with the landing.

note: Buttons record requests, sensors track position, the controller manages speed and direction, and safety devices keep watching the whole time.
